name: Mystical ecstasy and union with the One
plain_explanation: Plotinus describes personally undergoing a rare, overwhelming experience of stepping outside his own body and ordinary self, briefly touching or merging with the highest, divine reality -- an experience so far beyond ordinary thought that it cannot be described or reasoned about while it is actually happening, only reflected on afterward.
precise_definition: The direct, non-discursive apprehension of the One (or of nous) that Plotinus reports experiencing repeatedly in his own life, described as a state in which 'there is no power whatever to make any affirmation' and reasoning about the vision is possible only 'afterwards,' once ordinary consciousness resumes.
why_it_mattered: It represents, for Russell, philosophy's clearest ancient instance of the union of rigorous metaphysical system-building with genuinely experiential mysticism, and Russell singles out passages describing it as among the most purely beautiful in all philosophical literature, comparable to Dante's Paradiso.
historical_origin: Reported as Plotinus's own repeated personal experience, recorded in the Enneads (notably IV.8.1 and V.3.17, as cited by Russell via the McKenna translation).
examples: Plotinus's first-person account: 'Many times it has happened: Lifted out of the body into myself... beholding a marvellous beauty...'
The instruction attributed to him for achieving the vision: 'Cut away everything'
influence_on_later_thinkers: Feeds directly into the later Christian and medieval mystical tradition's vocabulary and conceptual structure for describing union with God.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Central to Plotinus's religious/philosophical practice and to his historical influence on Christian mysticism.
